title: Numeric Enum Traps and Unchecked Literal Unions
platform_conditions: Numeric enums survive into emitted JS as reverse-mapping objects; const enums are erased -- both behaviors are tsc emit rules, runtime is the compiled JavaScript
security_mechanism: A numeric enum parameter is only checked to be 'some number' at runtime: setRole(3.7) or setRole(-1) compiles when the caller holds the value as any/number, and because regular enums emit a lookup object, the runtime value never matches a declared member. const enums are fully erased, so a payload that claims a const-enum-typed field supplies any number with no runtime evidence. String literal unions used for roles or states have the same gap on the wire: the union exists only in the checker, so unvalidated 'admin' strings arrive from payloads and drive privilege checks.

source_sink_clues.source: Decoded request fields typed as numeric enums, const enums, or string literal unions without a runtime membership check.
source_sink_clues.sink: Functions taking enum/literal-union parameters fed from external data; privilege and state checks comparing against enum members

tracking_guards: Check every enum/literal-union value crossing the boundary is validated with a runtime membership test (a schema enum, Object.values includes, or exhaustive parse) before use; prefer string literal unions validated at parse time over numeric enums.
not_candidate_when: The enum value originates in server-side constants and never crosses deserialization, the value passed a validated schema enum parse, or the member cannot affect authorization.
synthetic_vulnerable_example: enum Role { User = 1, Admin = 2 }; function setRole(r: Role) { ... }
public_references: CWE-704: Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/704.html
